Header: Bactrocera cucurbitae , Bactrocera dorsalis (previously B. invadens ) Vidudu or Inzi wa matunda in Swahili

Prevention: Timely planting to avoid tomato ripening and harvesting period during mango or guava fruit ripening seasons because of migration of flies from the fruits of these trees into tomato fields.
Harvest fruits nearing ripening; do not wait to harvest until total ripening of fruits.
Collect all fallen fruits from below nearby fruit trees because they host many fruit fly larvae.
Collect any fallen tomato, because they may attract fruit flies, and may allow larval developments
Monitoring: Tomato fruits rot when larvae of fruit flies live and feed inside.
The fly adult is a small winged insect of nearly 1 cm in length.
It is like a house fly in shape but smaller, and its body is nicely coloured.
Look for adult flies on the flowers and fruits.
For early, detection, use commercial pheromone traps with trimedlure (TML), or cue lure (CL), or methyl eugenol (ME) attractants (3traps/ km2).
Follow infestation regularly, once flies are detected.
Inspect fruits for soft black spotted ovi- punctures on the fruits weekly.
Larvae enter the tomato and are yellowish whitish, 0.5 to 1 cm long, 2 to 3 mm thick.
When damage is detected on 1 to 2 tomatoes / 10 plants on average, consider acting quickly before more eggs are laid and hatching larvae feed inside tomatoes.
At high infestations, i.e. in case of mass invasion, your tomatoes are likely to be lost.
Direct Control: Grind 50 g wild basil leaves; soak overnight in 2-3 litres water; strain; add 10g soap; then spray over un-ripened tomatoes (reach coverage) early in the mornings.
Collect all mature rotten tomato fruits from the plants because they harbour fruit fly larvae.

Attract and trap flies by using fermented brew + little insecticide:
Cut a plastic water bottle it into 2 halves.
Fill fermented mango juice, cider vinegar, fermented banana, other fermented fruit juice or local brews into ¼ the lower bottle.
You may add 2-5 drops of insecticides into the fermented juice.
Invert upper half of bottle and insert it like a funnel into lower half.
Hang traps into the lower canopy of nearby mango and guava trees that are at late flowering stage.
Place at least 10 traps per acre around tomato field.
The fermented juice attracts fruit flies which get down the funnel and fall into the juice.
This control method only works if many tomato and fruit tree farmers participate.
Chemical sprays cannot control fruit fly adult in tomatoes, because they migrate from neighbouring fruit trees.
Chemicals can also not control fruit fly larvae because the adults lay their eggs inside the tomato fruits, and larvae develop inside the fruit.
When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label.
Always consult recent list of registered pesticides (MAFC / TPRI).
WHO toxicity class
III (slightly hazardous); biological spinosyn pesticide; p.h.i. 3 d, r.e.i. 1 d, min retreatment 7 d, max 2 sprays per season at days without rain.
Avoid spraying at bright sunlight.
Very toxic to aquatic organisms.
